subject: maths

moments.title: VC dimension
moments.body: Vapnik and Chervonenkis develop a theory of machine learning generalisation based on the VC dimension. Soviet pure mathematics quietly underpins modern AI.
moments.takeaway: A formal theory of when ML generalises.

moments.title: Support vector machines
moments.who: Vladimir Vapnik et al., AT&T Bell Labs
moments.body: SVMs combine VC theory with kernels to give a state-of-the-art classifier. They dominate ML for a decade.
moments.takeaway: VC theory yields a practical algorithm.

moments.title: AlexNet
moments.body: AlexNet wins ImageNet by a wide margin using a deep convolutional network on GPUs. SVMs are dethroned. Deep learning is born — and largely outruns VC theory.
moments.takeaway: Deep learning works without the guarantees VC theory provides.

moments.title: Generalisation puzzle
moments.body: Deep nets have far more parameters than examples but generalise well. Why? Double descent, neural tangent kernel, mean-field theory — multiple theories vie.
moments.takeaway: Modern ML works better than theory predicts.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Statistical learning theory is a major sub-discipline. New theories try to explain why deep nets work. ML drives much of modern computational research.
now.open_questions: Why do deep nets generalise? What is the right theory?

reflection: Vapnik's VC theory remains beautiful and partially obsolete. How does theory cope when practice outruns it?
